flawed_step: A proof would need, for every n >= 4, a graph G with |E(G)| = |E(complement of G)|. Isomorphic graphs have the same number of edges, so this means |E(G)| = n(n-1)/4. That is an integer only when n ≡ 0 or 1 (mod 4). For n ≡ 2 or 3 (mod 4) the step cannot be justified.
counterexample: Take n = 6. K_6 has C(6,2) = 15 edges. If G has e edges on 6 vertices, its complement has 15 − e edges. An isomorphism keeps the edge count, so G ≅ complement(G) would need e = 15 − e, which gives e = 7.5. That is not an integer, so no self-complementary graph on 6 vertices exists. (n = 7 fails the same way: 21 edges would need e = 10.5.)
assessment_summary: The statement is false. A self-complementary graph on n vertices must have exactly n(n-1)/4 edges, so one can exist only when n ≡ 0 or 1 (mod 4). For n = 6 this count would be 15/2, which is not a whole number, so no such graph exists. The claim fails for n = 6.
